title: Simple Pendulum: L-T² graph and the second's pendulum
objective: To plot the L-T² graph for a simple pendulum.
To use the graph to find the effective length of a second's pendulum.
To determine the acceleration due to gravity, g, from the slope.

theory.statement: For small angular amplitude the bob of a simple pendulum executes simple harmonic motion with time period T = 2π√(L/g), where L is the effective length measured from the point of suspension to the centre of gravity of the bob.
theory.derivationNote: Squaring gives T² = (4π²/g)·L, so a graph of T² against L is a straight line through the origin whose slope is 4π²/g. Hence g = 4π²/slope. A second's pendulum has T = 2 s, so its length is read off the graph at T² = 4 s².

apparatus.name: Metallic bob with hook
apparatus.why: Heavy and small, so air resistance is negligible

apparatus.name: Cotton thread
apparatus.why: Light and inextensible so the length stays constant

apparatus.name: Split cork
apparatus.why: Grips the thread at one definite point of suspension

apparatus.name: Clamp and stand
apparatus.why: Provides a rigid support that does not vibrate

apparatus.name: Stop clock / stop watch
apparatus.why: Times a counted number of oscillations

apparatus.name: Vernier callipers
apparatus.why: Measures the bob diameter, half of which is added to the thread length

procedure.text: Measure the diameter of the bob with vernier callipers and note its radius r.
Set the effective length L (thread length + hook + radius of bob) using the length slider. Start at 60 cm.
Displace the bob through a small angle (not more than 15°) and release it gently so it swings in one vertical plane.
Allow a few oscillations to pass, then start the stop clock as the bob crosses the mean position.
Count 20 complete oscillations and stop the clock. Record the total time t.
Calculate T = t/n and T². Enter the reading in the observation table.
Repeat for at least five more lengths, increasing L by about 10 cm each time.
Plot L on the x-axis against T² on the y-axis and draw the best-fit straight line through the origin.
Find the slope, calculate g = 4π²/slope, and read the length at T² = 4 s² to get the second's pendulum.

steps: Slope of the L-T² graph = ΔT²/ΔL
Second's pendulum: read L at T² = 4 s²

expectedResult.statement: The L-T² graph is a straight line through the origin, showing T² ∝ L. The value of g obtained is close to 9.8 m·s⁻² and the second's pendulum is about 99 cm long.

safety: Clamp the stand firmly to the table so it cannot topple while the bob swings.
Keep the amplitude small (under 15°) — a wildly swinging bob can strike a neighbour or the stand.
Ensure nobody is standing in the plane of oscillation.
Use a bob with a secure hook; check the knot before releasing.
sourcesOfError: Reaction time while starting and stopping the clock (reduced by timing 20 oscillations instead of one).
Amplitude larger than 15° makes the motion non-simple-harmonic and increases T.
The bob spinning or moving in an ellipse instead of a plane.
Yielding of the support or a stretchable thread changing the effective length.
Error in locating the centre of gravity of the bob.

viva.question: What is a simple pendulum?
viva.expectedConcept: An ideal simple pendulum is a heavy point mass suspended by a weightless, inextensible, perfectly flexible string from a rigid, frictionless support.
viva.commonMisconception: Describing the laboratory arrangement without mentioning that the ideal bob is a point mass.

viva.question: What is meant by the effective length of a pendulum?
viva.expectedConcept: The distance from the point of suspension to the centre of gravity of the bob, i.e. length of thread + length of hook + radius of the bob.

viva.question: Why do we time 20 oscillations instead of one?
viva.expectedConcept: The error due to reaction time is divided by the number of oscillations, so the error in T becomes 20 times smaller.
viva.commonMisconception: Saying it is 'more accurate' without explaining that the error is divided by n.

viva.question: Does the time period depend on the mass of the bob? Justify.
viva.expectedConcept: No. T = 2π√(L/g) contains no mass term, because the restoring force and the inertia both scale with mass and cancel.
viva.answerLogic: mg sinθ restoring force divided by m inertia.
viva.commonMisconception: Believing a heavier bob swings faster or slower.

viva.question: What is a second's pendulum and how long is it?
viva.expectedConcept: A pendulum whose time period is exactly 2 seconds; its length is about 99.2 cm (approximately 1 m) at g = 9.8 m·s⁻².
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking a second's pendulum takes 1 second for a full oscillation — it takes 1 s for each half swing.

viva.question: Why must the amplitude be kept small?
viva.expectedConcept: Only for small angles is sin θ ≈ θ, which makes the restoring force proportional to displacement and the motion simple harmonic. For large amplitudes T increases.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking amplitude never affects the period at any angle.

viva.question: What will happen to the time period of a pendulum taken to the Moon?
viva.expectedConcept: g on the Moon is about 1/6 of that on Earth, so T increases by a factor of √6, about 2.45 times.
viva.commonMisconception: Saying it becomes 6 times longer instead of √6.

viva.question: The graph between L and T² is a straight line. What does its slope represent?
viva.expectedConcept: The slope equals 4π²/g, so g can be calculated as 4π² divided by the slope.
viva.commonMisconception: Reading the slope as g itself.

viva.question: If the pendulum bob is replaced by a hollow sphere filled with water that slowly leaks out, what happens to T?
viva.expectedConcept: The centre of gravity first moves down (T increases), then rises back as the sphere empties (T decreases), returning to the original value.
viva.answerLogic: Effective length follows the centre of gravity.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming T only increases because mass is lost.

preLab.question: The effective length of a simple pendulum is measured up to:
options: The centre of gravity of the bob
preLab.feedback: The effective length runs from the point of suspension to the centre of gravity of the bob, so the radius of the bob must be added.

preLab.question: Which apparatus fixes a definite point of suspension?
preLab.feedback: The split cork grips the thread so the pendulum swings about one fixed point.

preLab.question: The amplitude of oscillation should not exceed about:
preLab.feedback: Beyond roughly 15° the approximation sin θ ≈ θ fails and the motion stops being simple harmonic.

duringLab.question: Record readings for at least five different lengths.
Keep the amplitude at or below 15° for every reading.
Show that changing the mass of the bob does not change T.

postLab.question: From your graph, state the value of g you obtained (m·s⁻²).
postLab.feedback: The accepted value at this latitude is about 9.79 m·s⁻².

postLab.question: State the length of the second's pendulum from your graph (cm).
postLab.feedback: L = gT²/4π² with T = 2 s gives about 99 cm.

postLab.question: Your L-T² graph passes through the origin. What does this prove?
options: T² is inversely proportional to L
postLab.feedback: A straight line through the origin means direct proportionality between the plotted quantities, i.e. T² ∝ L.

assumptions: Amplitude below 15° so sin θ ≈ θ
scientificValidation.validRange: L = 0.20 m to 1.50 m; amplitude ≤ 15°; mass 20-200 g
scientificValidation.unitSystem: SI; bench measurements in cm and s, converted to m for the graph
edgeCases: L below 20 cm: bob radius no longer negligible — blocked
Amplitude above 15°: period rises by the factor (1 + θ₀²/16)
Very large n: total time exceeds a practical lab period
expectedBehaviour: g recovered within 3% from noisy quantised data
